# Steel bridge inspection

This field note explains fatigue cracks in steel bridges. Its central process is repeated stress cycles at welds and bolted connections. Practitioners pay attention to the surrounding conditions before interpreting a single observation. A useful working method involves close visual inspection followed by magnetic particle testing. This is not simply a matter of collecting a number: observations need enough context to distinguish a persistent pattern from a temporary change.

An important interpretation is that small cracks can grow under loads well below ultimate strength. For a practical assessment, document when and where the observation was made, the equipment or materials involved, and any unusual conditions. Compare measurements taken using the same method rather than assuming that unrelated measurements are directly comparable. Recording changes over time also helps explain whether an intervention is having its intended effect.

There is an important limitation: paint damage alone does not prove structural failure. When conditions change, revisit the original assumptions instead of applying the same response automatically. A careful operator checks equipment, records the relevant circumstances, and looks for independent evidence before drawing conclusions. Reports should distinguish what was observed from what is inferred and describe any uncertainty that could affect the decision.

The best procedure depends on the actual situation and the people responsible for it. Where a result has consequences for safety, conservation, or expensive equipment, use the appropriate local guidance and consult a qualified specialist. The examples in this note illustrate the principles rather than providing an exhaustive operating manual.
